task_description: Discovering small-molecule organic solid-state laser (OSL) gain materials with best-in-class emission gain cross section in solution and amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) threshold in thin-film devices, by iteratively selecting, synthesizing, and characterizing candidates from a combinatorial chemical space of >150,000 pentameric structures built from modular cap, bridge, and core building blocks.

datasets.db_description: A curated experimental dataset containing synthesis outcomes, spectroscopic characterization data (absorption/emission spectra, photoluminescence quantum yield, lifetime), and computed emission gain cross sections (σ_em) for 287 experimentally realized pentameric OSL candidates. It includes molecular structures (SMILES), building block identities, reaction conditions, HPLC-MS traces, and quality-controlled optical measurements. This dataset was used to train and validate the Gaussian process regressor (with GNN embeddings) for Bayesian optimization of new high-gain candidates.

A large-scale computational dataset generated via time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) with vertical-gradient approximation, containing excited-state properties (e.g., S1 energy, oscillator strength, vibronic coupling parameters) for ~92,880 molecules sampled across the full >150,000 candidate space. These simulated descriptors were used to pretrain a graph neural network (GNN) whose learned embeddings served as input features for predicting experimental σ_em — enabling physics-informed surrogate modeling where experimental data was sparse.

A physical and digital library of 32 cap, 30 bridge, and 161 core building blocks — including commercially sourced compounds and custom-synthesized TIDA-protected haloarylboronic acids and pinacol boronic esters — defining the discrete, synthesizable search space for pentameric OSL candidates. The library enabled enumeration of >150,000 target molecules and directly constrained the active search space for Bayesian optimization based on real-time availability across distributed labs.
